Incoming New Jersey Congressman Who Volunteered With Al-Qaeda Front Group Set To Speak At Alleged Hamas-Linked Conference

November 26, 2026 5:48 pm
4

By Reuven Rosenfeld

NEW YORK (VINnews) — Newly elected Democratic Rep. Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, who once volunteered with a charity later shut down as an al-Qaeda front, is scheduled to address a conference hosted by a group facing lawsuits and congressional scrutiny over alleged ties to Hamas.

Join our WhatsApp group

Subscribe to our Daily Roundup Email

Hamawy, a 56-year-old Egyptian-born plastic and reconstructive surgeon and former Army trauma surgeon, won election in November to represent New Jersey’s 12th Congressional District. He succeeds retiring Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman and will become the state’s first Muslim member of Congress when he is sworn in in January.

In the summer of 1994, shortly after medical school, Hamawy spent roughly five weeks in Bosnia with the Chicago-based Benevolence International Foundation. In a 1996 interview with the Newark Star-Ledger, he described working in Sarajevo and Zenica to assess hospital needs and deliver supplies. U.S. authorities later determined the group provided logistical and financial support to al-Qaeda. The 9/11 Commission Report characterized its Bosnia operations as part of a network that covertly aided terrorist activities linked to Osama bin Laden. Offices in Sarajevo and Zenica were raided in 2002 as part of a joint U.S.-Bosnian effort; the group was subsequently shut down. Hamawy was never charged in connection with the organization.

Hamawy also had a documented association with Sheikh Omar Abdel-Rahman, known as the Blind Sheikh. He met the cleric in New Jersey in 1991, attended lectures and events with him, assisted with translation, and testified as a defense witness at Abdel-Rahman’s 1995 federal trial. Abdel-Rahman was convicted of seditious conspiracy in connection with plots linked to the 1993 World Trade Center bombing; he died in 2017. Hamawy has described his testimony as a matter of civic duty and has not been accused of criminal involvement.

Hamawy is listed to speak on two panels at the Palestine Convention, organized by American Muslims for Palestine (AMP) and underway this week near Chicago. One panel addresses post-2026 election analysis and legislative strategy for the next Congress; the other covers political opportunities and challenges within the major parties. AMP has faced a long-running civil lawsuit from the family of David Boim, an American killed by Hamas in 1996, alleging that the group is essentially a successor to earlier organizations found liable for supporting the terrorist group. House and Senate committees have also investigated AMP leadership over alleged Hamas connections. Other scheduled speakers include activist Linda Sarsour and former Rep. Cori Bush of Missouri.

Hamawy has been an outspoken critic of Israel, describing its military operations in Gaza as genocide, and volunteered as a physician there in 2024 and 2025. His campaign has previously characterized scrutiny of his past associations as Islamophobic guilt by association. Neither Hamawy nor AMP representatives responded to the New York Post’s requests for comment on the conference appearance.

The incoming lawmaker’s participation comes amid heightened focus on his record and foreign-policy positions as he prepares to take office.
